27-053.r: Right to travel abroad as personal liberty → Maneka Gandhi (1978), not Bella Banerjee (land case, 1948 Act); Indira Sawhney → OBC creamy layer; Vishaka → workplace sexual harassment.
27-053.t: Bella Banerjee is a land development law case; travel abroad belongs to Maneka Gandhi.

27-054.r: Supreme Court jurisdiction → Original (Article 131), Appellate (Articles 132-136) and Advisory (Article 143).
27-054.h: Numbers rise with the order: 131 original, 132-136 appeal, 143 advice.

27-055.r: Collegium system, appellate and original jurisdiction → all relate to Supreme Court; collegium evolved through SC judgments, not by an Act or the Constitution.

27-056.r: Appellate jurisdiction in constitutional cases → Article 132 read with Article 134A (appeals from High Courts); Article 131 → original jurisdiction.

27-057.r: Cases on interpretation of the Constitution reach the Supreme Court under its Appellate Jurisdiction (appeals from High Courts in civil, criminal or other cases).

27-058.r: Curative Petition → evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra vs Ashok Hurra (2002); filed in Supreme Court under Article 142.

27-059.r: Article 137 → Supreme Court can review its own judgment or order, subject to law made by Parliament and rules under Article 145.

27-061.r: Supreme Court can change (review) its own judgment under Article 137, subject to law by Parliament and rules under Article 145.

27-062.r: Article 142 → SC can pass any decree or order for complete justice, enforceable across India; ordinary laws cannot limit it, so SC is not constrained by Parliament's laws.

27-063.r: Judicial Review → power of Judiciary to interpret the Constitution and declare laws or executive orders void if they conflict with it.

27-066.r: Constitution doesn't define 'basic structure' (doctrine first recognised in Kesavananda Bharati case, 1973); it does provide judicial review to protect rights (Article 13 voids laws violating Part III).

27-067.r: Judicial Review in India → both Supreme Court and High Courts; originated in USA, Marbury vs Madison (1803), CJ John Marshall; declared part of basic structure.

27-068.r: 42nd Amendment (1976) barred High Courts from judging validity of Central laws; 43rd Amendment (1977) restored it; SC can examine constitutional amendments; both statements false.

27-069.r: Judicial Review → exists in both India (Article 13) and USA; not in UK, where Parliament is supreme and its laws cannot be challenged in court.

27-070.r: Judicial review in India is limited (mainly checks laws touching basic structure); Constitution is a 'bag of borrowings'; both true, but R does not explain A.

27-071.r: Due Process of Law → in essence the principle of natural justice (fairness, no arbitrariness); natural justice includes 'Nemo judex in causa sua' (no one judges own cause).
27-071.t: Don't pick 'procedure established by law'; due process is about fairness, i.e. natural justice.

27-072.r: Judicial review in India → based on 'Procedure established by Law'; found in Articles 13, 32, 136, 137, 226, 227.
27-072.t: Don't pick 'Due Process of Law'; Indian judicial review rests on procedure established by law.
hi: Procedure established by law (विधि द्वारा स्थापित प्रक्रिया)

27-073.r: Judicial process in India → based on the Constitution, procedure established by law, conventions and due process of routine law; so 'more than one' is correct.

27-074.r: Amendment moving Right to Equality before law out of Part III → can be struck down (Article 13(2): no law may take away or abridge Part III rights).

27-075.r: Supreme Court → highest court, guarantor of Fundamental Rights and guardian of the Constitution; so 'more than one of the above' is correct.

27-076.r: Final authority to interpret the Constitution → Supreme Court; it is the Guardian or Custodian of the Constitution.
hi: Guardian of the Constitution (संविधान का संरक्षक)

27-079.r: Custodian / Guardian of the Constitution of India → Supreme Court (not President, PM or Lok Sabha Secretariat).

27-081.r: SC has no exclusive jurisdiction on validity of Central laws (High Courts too; writs under Articles 32 and 226); SC is Guardian of the Constitution → A false, R true.

27-082.r: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights → both Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226); HC writ power is wider (also other rights).

27-083.r: Article 32 → Right to Constitutional Remedies; Supreme Court issues directions, orders, writs to enforce Fundamental Rights (Part III).
hi: Right to Constitutional Remedies (संवैधानिक उपचारों का अधिकार)

27-084.r: Enlarging Supreme Court's jurisdiction on Union List matters → Parliament by law (Article 138(1)).

27-085.r: Supreme Court's jurisdiction can be enlarged by Parliament by making a law (Article 138).
27-085.t: It needs a law, not a mere resolution of Parliament or a Presidential order.

27-086.r: Advisory opinion of Supreme Court on a question of law → sought by the President (Article 143), not PM or High Courts.

27-087.r: Article 143(1) → President can refer to Supreme Court a question of law or fact of public importance, e.g. appointment and transfer of Judges.

27-088.r: Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143) → heard by a bench of 5; opinion not binding on government; SC must answer only references on old treaties/agreements, not other questions.

27-090.r: Supreme Court advises the President on law or fact of public importance only when he seeks it (Article 143(1)), never on its own.

27-092.r: Gujarat Assembly election deferment (2002) → President Abdul Kalam sought SC's advice under Article 143 on Election Commission powers (Articles 324, 174).

27-093.r: Oath to 'bear true faith and allegiance... uphold the Constitution and the laws' → Chief Justice of India; Third Schedule has 10 forms of oaths/affirmations.

27-094.r: Article 139A → Supreme Court can transfer cases anywhere in India (e.g. same question of law pending in several High Courts).

27-095.r: A.K. Gopalan → preventive detention procedure; Romesh Thapar → restrictions on free speech; Shankari Prasad → Parliament's power to amend; Champakam Dorairajan → equal admission to educational institutions.
27-095.c: No answer printed (*): the given codes do not seem to match the correct pairs.

27-096.r: Zamindari cases (book: all four) → Kameshwar Singh vs Bihar, Ramesh Thaper vs Madras, Motilal vs UP, West Bengal vs Subodh Gopal.
27-096.c: Book says all four, but in another question it calls Romesh Thapar vs Madras a free-speech case; the answer looks doubtful.

27-097.r: Indra Sawhney vs Union of India (1992) → OBC reservation in government jobs; reservation under Articles 15(4), 16(4) not to exceed 50 per cent.

27-098.r: Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983 → struck down by SC (13 July 2005) under Article 355; migration from Bangladesh called aggression on Assam.

27-099.r: TDSAT (set up 2000 by amending TRAI Act, 1997) → its judgments can be challenged in High Court and Supreme Court.

27-100.r: Shortest CJI tenure → Kamal Narain Singh (25.11.1991 to 12.12.1991), shorter than G.B. Pattanaik, S. Rajendra Babu, R.M. Lodha.

27-101.r: CJI sequence → H.L. Dattu → T.S. Thakur → Jagdish Singh Khehar; earlier S.R. Das → B.P. Sinha → P.B. Gajendragadkar; K.G. Balakrishnan → S.H. Kapadia.

27-102.r: Y.V. Chandrachud → 16th Chief Justice of India (22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985), longest-serving CJI; appointed by President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy.

27-103.r: Justice M. Fathima Beevi (died 23 November 2023) → first woman SC Judge (1989); first Muslim woman in higher judiciary; Governor of Tamil Nadu 1997-2001.
27-103.t: She was Governor of Tamil Nadu, not Kerala.

27-104.r: A.S. Anand (Adarsh Sein Anand) → 29th Chief Justice of India, 10 October 1998 to 31 October 2001.

27-105.r: Justice Fathima Beevi → India's first woman Judge of the Supreme Court; also first Muslim woman Governor (Tamil Nadu).

27-106.r: Justice Gyan Sudha Misra → fourth woman SC Judge (30 April 2010), earlier Patna HC Chief Justice; before her Fathima Beevi, Sujata Manohar, Ruma Pal; fifth: Ranjana Prakash Desai.
27-106.h: Order of women SC Judges: Fathima, Sujata, Ruma, Gyan, Ranjana.

27-107.r: L. Nageshwara Rao → elevated directly from the Bar to Supreme Court (7th such person), sworn in 13 May 2016; never a High Court judge.

27-108.r: Justice N. Kotiswar Singh → Chief Justice of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court before SC (oath 18 July 2024); Justice Manmohan (ex-Delhi HC CJ) sworn 5 December 2024.

27-109.r: Among MP High Court Chief Justices, S.K. Jha never became a Supreme Court Judge; A.K. Patnaik, R.V. Raveendran, A.K. Mathur did.

27-110.r: R.C. Lahoti (35th CJI, 1 June 2004 to 1 November 2005) → never a Rajasthan High Court judge; joined the Bar at Guna (MP) in 1960.

27-111.r: First PIL → Hussainara Khatoon vs State of Bihar (1979), taken up by Justice P.N. Bhagwati; CJI then was Y.V. Chandrachud; Bhagwati later 17th CJI.
27-111.c: No answer printed (*): the CJI at that time, Y.V. Chandrachud, is not among the options.

27-112.r: Public Interest Litigation → introduced by judicial initiative after the Emergency era; in line with Article 39A (social justice); any public person or NGO can approach court.

27-116.r: PIL → judge-made process that widened locus standi, giving weaker sections access to justice (R true); calling it 'essential for rule of law' is treated as false (A false).

27-117.r: PIL → public-minded citizens can approach court for those unable to reach it themselves; A and R true, R explains A.

27-118.r: Public Interest Litigation → originated in the United States (legal aid movement; first legal aid office in New York, 1876).
27-118.t: Not India or UK: the PIL concept began in the United States.
